![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14275251/assets/e6c13f4405c407123973c370a20c88b9c989bd54ade909b06414eabc22f0d45e.png)

Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨x,\,y,\,z⟩$ and the boundary $S$ of a spherical solid of radius $1$ centered at the origin. Calculate the flux of $F$ through $S.$
questions.worked_solution:
If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

For a sphere or radius $r$ centered at $O,$ the unit normal to the sphere is given by

$$
n=\frac{⟨x,y,z⟩}{r}.
$$

In our case, we have $r=1.$ Therefore,

$$
n=⟨x,y,z⟩.
$$

Using the fact that ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}=1$ on $S,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot n & =⟨x,\,y,\,z⟩\cdot ⟨x,y,z⟩ \\  & ={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across $S$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{S}1\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S \\  & =\text{Area}(S) \\  & =4\pi \cdot {1}^{2} \\  & =4\pi \end{aligned}
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14275251/assets/cece4e226becb315d6d951a8ae782750da79209d9a67ec52a8cd4d134999e9e6.png)

Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨0,\,0,\,z(4-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2})⟩$ and the surface $S$ defined by the bounding region of a right circular cylinder of height $4$ whose base is a circle of radius $3$ centered at the origin, as shown above. Calculate the flux of $F$ through $S.$
questions.worked_solution:
If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

Notice that only the $z$-component of $F=⟨0,\,0,\,z(4-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2})⟩$ is non-zero. Since the lateral side of $S$ is parallel to the $z$-axis, the flux of $F$ through $S$ will be non-zero only at the top and bottom sides. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14275251/assets/21e29d99d2d5330db2d946d981e4bd0f820ce26297bf95f962cb3000f0998136.png)

 
Let's consider the flux of $F$ through these two sides.

- Let ${S}_{1}$ denote the top surface. On this surface, we have $z=4$ for ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\le 9.$ The outward-pointing unit normal vector to ${S}_{1}$ is

$$
{n}_{1}=⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩.
$$

Using the fact that $z=4$ on ${S}_{1},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot {n}_{1} & =⟨0,\,0,\,z(4-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2})⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,0,\,4(4-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2})⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩ \\  & =4(4-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the flux of $F$ across ${S}_{1}$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}4(4-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2})\,\text{d}S \\  & =4{∬}_{D}4-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying a change of variables $(x,y)\to (r,\theta ),\text{d}A=r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta ,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}4{∬}_{D}4-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}\,\text{d}A & =4{∬}_{D}(4-{r}^{2})\,r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{3}4r-{r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}\theta {\int }_{0}^{3}4r-{r}^{3}\,\text{d}r \\  & =4\cdot 2\pi \cdot {[2{r}^{2}-\frac{1}{4}{r}^{4}]}_{0}^{3} \\  & =8\pi \cdot (18-\frac{81}{4}) \\  & =-18\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

- Let ${S}_{2}$ denote the bottom surface. On this surface, we have $z=0$ for ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\le 9.$ Therefore, for everywhere on ${S}_{2},$ we have

$$
F(x,y,0)=⟨0,\,0,\,0(4-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2})⟩=⟨0,\,0,\,0⟩.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}0\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}0\,\text{d}S \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S+{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & =-18\pi +0 \\  & =-18\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨0,\,0,\,{x}^{2}-yz⟩$ and the surface $S$ defined by the bounding region of the rectangular solid shown above in the first octant. Calculate the flux of $F$ through $S.$
questions.worked_solution:
If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

Notice that only the $z$-component of $F=⟨0,\,0,\,{x}^{2}-yz⟩$ is non-zero. Since the lateral sides of $S$ are parallel to the $z$-axis, the flux of $F$ through $S$ will be non-zero only at the top and bottom sides. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14275251/assets/fdaad0039f4b7fea5c6e301f4cc3b89687f5f4081e3bd87f8ce31daacda2744b.png)

 

Let's consider the flux of $F$ through these two sides.

- Let ${S}_{1}$ denote the top surface. On this surface, we have $z=2$ for $0\le x\le 3$ and $0\le y\le 2.$ The outward-pointing unit normal vector to ${S}_{1}$ is

$$
{n}_{1}=⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩.
$$

Using the fact that $z=2$ on ${S}_{1},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot {n}_{1} & =⟨0,\,0,\,{x}^{2}-yz⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,0,\,{x}^{2}-2y⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩ \\  & ={x}^{2}-2y.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across ${S}_{1}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}{x}^{2}-2y\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}-2y\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{3}{x}^{2}-2y\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{[\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}-2xy]}_{x=0}^{x=3}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}9-6y\,\text{d}y \\  & ={[9y-3{y}^{2}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

- Let ${S}_{2}$ denote the bottom surface. On this surface, we have $z=0$ for $0\le x\le 3$ and $0\le y\le 2.$ The outward-pointing unit normal vector to ${S}_{2}$ is

$$
{n}_{2}=⟨0,\,0,\,-1⟩.
$$

Using the fact that $z=0$ on ${S}_{2},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot {n}_{2} & =⟨0,\,0,\,{x}^{2}-yz⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,-1⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,0,\,{x}^{2}⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,-1⟩ \\  & =-{x}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across ${S}_{2}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}-{x}^{2}\,\text{d}S \\  & =-{∬}_{D}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}A \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{3}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{2}{[\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}]}_{x=0}^{x=3}\,\text{d}y \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{2}9\,\text{d}y \\  & =-9[y]_{0}^{2} \\  & =-18.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S+{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & =6+(-18) \\  & =-12.\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨x-z,\,y,\,z+x⟩$ and the boundary $S$ of a spherical solid of radius $2$ centered at the origin. Calculate the flux of $F$ through $S.$
questions.worked_solution:
If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

For a sphere or radius $r$ centered at $O,$ the unit normal to the sphere is given by

$$
n=\frac{⟨x,y,z⟩}{r}.
$$

In our case, we have $r=2.$ Therefore,

$$
n=\frac{1}{2}⟨x,y,z⟩.
$$

Using the fact that ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}=4$ on $S,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot n & =⟨x-z,\,y,\,z+x⟩\cdot \frac{1}{2}⟨x,y,z⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{2}⟨x-z,\,y,\,z+x⟩\cdot ⟨x,y,z⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(x(x-z)+{y}^{2}+z(z+x)) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}({x}^{2}-xz+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}+xz) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 4 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across $S$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{S}2\,\text{d}S \\  & =2{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S \\  & =2\cdot \text{Area}(S) \\  & =2\cdot 4\pi \cdot {2}^{2} \\  & =32\pi \end{aligned}
$$

Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨8{x}^{2}({y}^{2}+{z}^{2}),\,0,\,0⟩$ and the surface $S$ defined by the bounding region of a right circular cylinder of height $1$ whose base is a circle of radius $2$ centered at the origin, as shown above. Calculate the flux of $F$ through $S.$
questions.worked_solution:
If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

Notice that only the $x$-component of $F=⟨8{x}^{2}({y}^{2}+{z}^{2}),\,0,\,0⟩$ is non-zero. Since the lateral side of $S$ is parallel to the $x$-axis, the flux of $F$ through $S$ will be non-zero only at the front and back sides. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14275251/assets/e4488f9fbf8c16883ac2470544d5fadcb63b2bff362b25a41a8a70bfe48232a2.png)

Let's consider the flux of $F$ through these two sides.

- Let ${S}_{1}$ denote the front surface. On this surface, we have $x=1$ for ${y}^{2}+{z}^{2}\le 4.$ The outward-pointing unit normal vector to ${S}_{1}$ is

$$
{n}_{1}=⟨1,\,0,\,0⟩.
$$

Using the fact that $x=1$ on ${S}_{1},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot {n}_{1} & =⟨8{x}^{2}({y}^{2}+{z}^{2}),\,0,\,0⟩\cdot ⟨1,\,0,\,0⟩ \\  & =⟨8({1}^{2})({y}^{2}+{z}^{2}),\,0,\,0⟩\cdot ⟨1,\,0,\,0⟩ \\  & =⟨8({y}^{2}+{z}^{2}),\,0,\,0⟩\cdot ⟨1,\,0,\,0⟩ \\  & =8({y}^{2}+{z}^{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the flux of $F$ across ${S}_{1}$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}8({y}^{2}+{z}^{2})\,\text{d}S \\  & =8{∬}_{D}({y}^{2}+{z}^{2})\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying a change of variables $(y,z)\to (r,\theta ),\text{d}A=r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta ,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}8{∬}_{D}({y}^{2}+{z}^{2})\,\text{d}A & =8{∬}_{D}{r}^{2}\cdot r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =8{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{2}{r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =8{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\text{d}\theta {\int }_{0}^{2}{r}^{3}\,\text{d}r \\  & =8\cdot 2\pi \cdot {[\frac{1}{4}{r}^{4}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =16\pi \cdot 4 \\  & =64\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

- Let ${S}_{2}$ denote the back surface. On this surface, we have $x=0$ for ${y}^{2}+{z}^{2}\le 4.$ Therefore, for everywhere on ${S}_{2},$ we have

$$
F(0,y,z)=⟨8({0}^{2})({y}^{2}+{z}^{2}),\,0,\,0⟩=⟨0,\,0,\,0⟩.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}0\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}0\,\text{d}S \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S+{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & =64\pi +0 \\  & =64\pi .\end{aligned}
$$
